title: Coarse cloth, jade inside
hook: the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside (Tao Te Ching 70)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a foot back: better to give up a foot than push forward an inch. Your line was a foot back.

A plain wool coat, a little frayed at the cuff. Nobody on the bus looks at it twice. Sewn into the lining, out of sight, is a small stone worth more than everything else the wearer owns. The coat isn't a disguise; it's just a coat. What matters is simply somewhere else. Chapter seventy of the Tao Te Ching ends on a picture very like that, and it gets there by way of a complaint.
screen: `A PLAIN COAT.` → `SOMETHING SEWN INSIDE.` → `THE CHAPTER'S COMPLAINT.`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practice, the speaker says, and yet nobody in the world understands them or practices them. A strange thing for a book to admit about itself: the teaching is simple, and it still goes unused. Second, the reason. Words have an ancestor and deeds have a master, something they come from. People who don't know that root, the chapter says, don't know me either. Those who know me are few, and that makes what I carry precious. Third, the picture. So the sage wears coarse cloth, the rough garment of a laborer, and holds jade at the breast, the precious stone riding close to the body under cheap fabric. Notice what the chapter doesn't say. It doesn't say the sage hides the jade out of fear, or shows it off to the right people. The outside is plain, the inside precious, and the two don't have to match. Fourth, the jade in a life. Some of what's most valuable doesn't photograph well: a promise kept for years, a habit of noticing who's left out, a sentence someone said to you once that still steadies you. None of it needs a better coat. And a treasure that's always on display can start to be about the display. The question it leaves: what's your jade, and does it need anyone's eyes on it?
screen: `EASY WORDS, RARELY USED.` · `FEW KNOW THE ROOT.` · `PLAIN OUTSIDE, JADE INSIDE.` · `WHAT'S YOUR JADE?` · then, large: `COARSE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly: what's one good thing in my life I don't need to announce? A kindness you're doing, something you're learning, a thing you love that nobody else much cares about. Hold it without telling anyone, the way the sage holds jade under a rough coat, and if the urge to share it rises, let it settle.
Coarse cloth. Chapter seventy's picture of the sage: rough, plain clothing outside, precious jade carried close inside. Today's word.
Your line: jade inside. The coat can stay plain. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy's image of the sage, plain cloth outside and jade inside, as a picture of a life whose real worth is carried quietly rather than displayed.

chat.says: What does it mean that the sage wears coarse cloth but holds jade inside?
options: Plain on the outside, precious inside: what's most valuable doesn't need to be on show.
It means the sage hides his treasure because he's afraid someone might steal it.
It means wise people should dress poorly so others will see how humble they are.
chat.meaning: Chapter seventy pictures the sage in coarse cloth holding jade at the breast: plain outside, precious inside, not hidden out of fear or shown off.

Tao Te Ching.meaning: the short Chinese classic of the Way, traditionally credited to Lao-tzu

jade.meaning: a hard, precious stone long treasured in China

sage.meaning: the wise person the Tao Te Ching holds up as a model

coarse cloth.meaning: rough, cheap fabric, the kind a laborer wears
